title: Ezra Reads, the People Understand
hook: learning to read a verse, a prayer, a page
carry: prayer counts in any language; hebrew opens it
tomorrow: two people, one text, and something rests between them. what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a page a day, or a line a day, gathered little by little. Any pace counts. Today, the language the page is written in.
screen: `ANY PACE COUNTS.` → `THE LANGUAGE ON THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: A form on a college portal asks you to rate your languages: reading, speaking, writing. Next to Hebrew, some people would have to write: by sound only. They can read the letters aloud in a prayer book and not know what most of the words mean. So can you pray in a language you barely read? The Mishnah answers plainly: yes.
screen: `RATE YOUR LANGUAGES.` → `HEBREW: BY SOUND ONLY.` → `THE MISHNAH: YES.`

segments.voice: It lists things that may be said in any language: the Shema, the prayer, the grace after meals. A prayer you understand counts. So why learn more Hebrew at all? The book of Nehemiah tells of a day when Ezra read the Torah aloud to the people in Jerusalem, and readers explained it, giving the sense, so the people understood what they heard. Reading and understanding, together. More Hebrew is how those two meet in one person. You start with words you already say. Shalom: peace. Torah: teaching. Emet: truth. Chesed: kindness. Lev: heart. Five words, and a page of the prayer book begins to light up in places. A verse becomes something you hear, not only something you sound out. Nobody has to be fluent for that. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Mishnah says the Shema may be said in any language. And still people keep learning Hebrew, a word at a time, because each word is a small way in.
screen: `ANY LANGUAGE COUNTS.` · `EZRA READS; THEY GIVE THE SENSE.` · `FIVE WORDS YOU ALREADY SAY.` · `A PAGE LIGHTS UP.` · then, large: `MORE HEBREW.`

segments.voice: Write five Hebrew words by hand, in English letters, each with its meaning: shalom, peace; Torah, teaching; emet, truth; chesed, kindness; lev, heart. Say each one once, out loud, as you write it. If you know the Hebrew letters, write one word in them too.
screen: `FIVE WORDS, BY HAND.` · `SAY EACH ONCE.` · `ONE IN HEBREW LETTERS, IF YOU CAN.`

segments.voice: More Hebrew: a few words at a time, until a verse, a prayer, a page is something you hear and understand, not only sound out.
Your line: prayer counts in any language, and Hebrew opens it, word by word. Shalom for now.

Shema.meaning: the declaration 'Hear, O Israel', said morning and evening

Mishnah.meaning: an early written collection of the rabbis' teachings

Ezra.meaning: a scribe who read the Torah aloud to the people

sources.ref: Mishnah Sotah 7:1 (these may be said in any language: the Shema, the prayer, the grace after meals, and others)
Nehemiah 8:1-8 (Ezra reads the Torah to the people; it is read distinctly and the sense is given, so they understand)

notes: Mishnah Sotah 7:1 paraphrased; the list is longer (the sotah passage, the confession of tithes, certain oaths); the script names three items.
Nehemiah 8:8 paraphrased; the script says 'readers explained it' (the Levites in the text).
Five words and their plain meanings (shalom, Torah, emet, chesed, lev); no root or etymology claims made.
Surprising fact: the Mishnah says the Shema may be said in any language.
